source.title: Contextures: Representations from Contexts
source.authors: Runtian Zhai; Kai Yang; Che-Ping Tsai; Burak Varici; Zico Kolter; P. Ravikumar

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws, but it does not test the claim’s held-out language-model loss laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream predictability. Its scaling experiment measures representation alignment, a related but different outcome.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws and reports an experiment varying neural-network width and depth, but measures alignment with top singular functions rather than held-out cross-entropy or any loss named in the claim versions. Those alignment results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. Cited scaling-law findings are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws and runs a width/depth sweep of small fully-connected networks on the tabular abalone dataset, but the outcome is representation alignment (CCA, mutual KNN) with kernel-PCA eigenfunctions, not held-out loss, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream performance versus scale. No power-law fit, extrapolation, or token/compute variation is reported. It measures a related but different construct, so it tests no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue scaling brings representations closer to the context's top-d singular functions, with diminishing or even negative returns once alignment is high. They conclude 'scaling is not all we need' and that better contexts are required. The declines are hypothesised to come from optimization difficulty at a fixed number of training steps.
record.recipe_differences: This is a representation-learning theory paper with an ablation of network width and depth on one dataset. It does not reproduce the language-model loss sweeps, fitting procedures, or compute-optimal allocation experiments in the cited scaling-law work.
record.method_sensitivity: In the abalone alignment experiment, width and depth affect alignment: increases help relatively narrow or shallow networks, while further increases can reduce it. The experiment uses the same number of training epochs across models; Appendix E describes full-batch AdamW and 15 random initializations per setting.

fits_no_version.finding: On abalone (KNN context, K=30, d=128, fixed training epochs), alignment of VICReg-trained MLP representations with exact top-d eigenfunctions rises with width and depth up to a point. It then declines, e.g. at depth 3 it peaks at width 512. Peak values are CCA about 0.9 and mutual KNN above 0.8.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling network width or depth improves alignment of learned representations with the context's top singular functions up to a point, after which returns diminish or reverse under a fixed training budget.

record.problems: The scaling-related experiment uses one dataset and measures representation alignment rather than language-model loss. The reported alignments are averages over 15 initializations, but no variability or error bars are stated. The authors themselves note possible optimization difficulty and that the exact optima are not reached.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results were found. The paper’s context-evaluation experiments and downstream prediction errors do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: All: no held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no fitted laws or extrapolation.
Loss at fixed parameter count across shapes. The width/depth sweep measures alignment and does not hold parameter count fixed.
All: no power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
Downstream error versus model scale. Downstream error is studied only versus context association and embedding dimension.
All: no exponent or allocation fitting.

record.verdict_notes: Theory paper on representation learning (ICML). The 'Implications for Scaling Laws' section is an argument, not a test of loss scaling. The training budget was fixed across sizes, so the non-monotonic trend confounds size with undertraining. No error bars are reported over the 15 seeds. Reader's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are kept.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Loss comparisons across architectures at fixed parameter count; the paper measures representation alignment, not loss.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance changing predictably with model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: fully-connected neural network
rows.size_stated: Embedding dimension d=128; depth and width varied. Appendix E describes training a 512-dimensional output and selecting its top 128 components.
rows.operation_detail: Vary neural-network width and depth while training a representation with VICReg implementing the non-contrastive objective.

conditions.value: 15 per width and depth; average alignment reported

rows.measure: CCA alignment with the exact top-d eigenfunctions
rows.baseline: Exact top-d eigenfunctions obtained by kernel PCA
rows.value: CCA can be as high as 0.9 when depth and width are chosen correctly
rows.note: Alignment is not a loss measure covered by the claim versions; the paper does not give the width and depth corresponding to this maximum in this statement.
rows.check: Peak-alignment summary statement (0.9 CCA). It is a best-case value at unspecified width/depth, and alignment is not a measure named by any version. Arguably a selection value rather than a scaling result.

rows.subject: fully-connected neural network
rows.size_stated: Embedding dimension d=128; depth and width varied. Appendix E describes training a 512-dimensional output and selecting its top 128 components.
rows.operation_detail: Vary neural-network width and depth while training a representation with VICReg implementing the non-contrastive objective.

conditions.value: 15 per width and depth; average alignment reported

rows.measure: Mutual KNN alignment with the exact top-d eigenfunctions
rows.baseline: Exact top-d eigenfunctions obtained by kernel PCA
rows.value: Mutual KNN alignment can be higher than 0.8 when depth and width are chosen correctly
rows.note: Alignment is not a loss measure covered by the claim versions; the paper does not give the width and depth corresponding to this value in this statement.
rows.check: Same issue as r1: peak mutual-KNN value (>0.8) at unspecified width/depth. It is not a loss or downstream-performance measure.

rows.subject: fully-connected neural network
rows.size_stated: Embedding dimension d=128; widths and depths varied. The text specifically compares depth 3 across widths and also compares depths at widths 512, 1024, and 2048.
rows.operation_detail: Increase network width or depth and measure representation alignment with the exact top-d eigenfunctions.
rows.measure: Representation alignment, measured using CCA and mutual KNN
rows.value: Increasing width improves alignment for relatively narrow networks, but after sufficient width it can reduce alignment; at depth 3, alignment is highest at width 512 and lower for widths above 512. Increasing depth shows a similar improvement-then-decline pattern; width 512 has higher alignment than widths 1024 and 2048 in the depth comparison.
rows.note: The paper hypothesizes that the declines reflect optimization difficulty under the same number of training steps. These are alignment results, not loss results covered by the claim versions.
rows.check: The non-monotonic alignment trend with width and depth is correctly recorded. It measures alignment, not loss. Training epochs were held fixed, so larger models are undertrained; authors attribute the decline to optimization.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
